title: US nursing-home roommate assignment changes mortality through patient peer effects
source_unit: US nursing-home stays, roommate cognitive status, private-room placement, patient diagnosis, and 90-day mortality

observations.period: Working paper issued December 2025; administrative records covering 2000–2010

denominator.unit: nursing-home stays across 7,200 US nursing homes

roommate_ad_90_day_mortality.unit: percentage-point increase in 90-day mortality relative to private-room placement for patients assigned a roommate with Alzheimer’s disease or related dementia

quality_equivalence.unit: standard deviation worse nursing-home quality equivalent in the reported mortality effect

ad_adrd_peer_benefit.unit: patients with Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias benefit substantially from cognitively healthy roommates but not from private rooms

non_ad_adrd_private_room.unit: mortality of patients without Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias is reduced in private rooms and does not depend on roommate cognitive health

assignment_rule.unit: percentage-point possible reduction in overall mortality from a simple assignment rule without additional resources

observations.method: Administrative records covering 2.6 million stays use unique room identifiers and plausibly exogenous roommate assignments to estimate patient peer effects and heterogeneous mortality responses.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract does not disclose all sample restrictions, confidence intervals, assignment assumptions, or implementation costs. The proposed 0.8 percentage-point reduction is a modeled assignment-rule estimate, not an implemented intervention; the study does not measure resident preferences, worker conditions, privacy, quality of life, or generalizability to current facilities.
observations.subgroup: Patients with and without Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias, assigned to roommates with different cognitive status or private rooms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Room assignment may still reflect unobserved clinical, staffing, family, or facility factors; mortality is not the whole resident experience, and a peer arrangement that benefits one subgroup can impose burden or privacy loss on another.

related_sources.claim: Medicaid financing can expand dementia volume toward lower-quality facilities and reduce one-year survival in the studied Indiana setting.
Inspection ratings predict relative nursing-home mortality while inspection responses are mostly temporary.
Nursing-home mergers reduce deficiency citations and direct-care hours without meaningful resident-health improvement.

boundary: This record adds a patient-peer and placement layer to the US nursing-home chain. It does not establish a universal roommate policy, disclose implementation costs, or measure privacy, resident preference, worker effects, quality of life, access, or current outcomes in the same unit.
